name: Radiomics
title: Radiomics
answer: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images, turning regions of interest into structured data for analysis. In diagnostic imaging and radiology, it is used to characterize tissue, predict treatment response, and support prognostic modeling, often alongside machine learning. The practice covers CT, MRI, PET, and other modalities, and it treats imaging as a source of mineable biomarkers rather than pictures for visual review alone.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images, turning regions of interest into structured data for analysis. In diagnostic imaging and radiology, it is used to characterize tissue, predict treatment response, and support prognostic modeling, often alongside machine learning. The practice covers CT, MRI, PET, and other modalities, and it treats imaging as a source of mineable biomarkers rather than pictures for visual review alone.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A radiomics workflow runs on DICOM images pulled from PACS or research archives, with segmentation performed in tools such as 3D Slicer or commercial radiotherapy software. Feature extraction typically uses open-source libraries like PyRadiomics, and model training may run on local workstations, hospital servers, or cloud instances with CPU or GPU resources. Storage and versioning of imaging cohorts, segmentations, and feature tables are part of the infrastructure, as is the need to manage large retrospective datasets.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with image acquisition and segmentation of a region of interest, followed by extraction of shape, first-order, texture, and filtered features. Features are then harmonized or normalized, reduced through selection or dimensionality reduction, and used to train and validate predictive models against clinical endpoints. Reproducibility depends on consistent imaging protocols, segmentation rules, and feature definitions, and external validation on independent cohorts is a standard check on overfitting.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Radiomics models inherit the governance obligations of medical AI, including patient privacy, data provenance, and regulatory review where the output informs care. Risks include bias from single-institution training data, scanner and protocol variability, and unclear accountability when a model contributes to a missed diagnosis or poor outcome. The field is documented alongside compliance and regulation pages and product liability tracking, reflecting the need for audit trails, validation evidence, and clear statements of intended use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Radiomics is moving toward prospective clinical trials, standardized feature definitions such as those from the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative, and tighter integration with radiology reporting and treatment planning. Federated learning and multi-institutional harmonization are expected to reduce site-specific bias, while radiogenomics and foundation models may link imaging features to molecular and genomic data. The longer-term direction is toward validated, regulatory-cleared imaging biomarkers that work across scanners and populations rather than single-center proof-of-concept models.
